titre: Herodotus and the Phoenix: Doubt Already Present in the Myth
accroche: Herodotus reports the Egyptian phoenix while warning that he himself does not believe it.
contenu_vulgarise:
Around 450 BCE, Herodotus visited Heliopolis, in Lower Egypt, and gathered from the people of Heliopolis the account of a bird he himself had only ever seen painted: the phoenix.

## What the People of Heliopolis Tell

According to their account, the bird shows itself in Egypt only once every five hundred years, at the death of its father. It then looks like an eagle, its plumage a mix of gold and red. What is told of its deeds, Herodotus writes, “does not seem credible to me”: it shapes with myrrh an egg as large as it can carry, hollows it out, lodges its father's body inside, plugs the opening with the myrrh it had removed, the egg then regaining its original weight, and carries the whole through the air from Arabia to the temple of the Sun at Heliopolis, where it deposits it.

Herodotus at no point claims to have witnessed the scene. He reports it in the mood of others: “it is said that,” “according to the people of Heliopolis.” And he sets down his own judgment even before laying out the feat: incredulous, he transmits it all the same, in full, because it belongs to what he was told about Egypt, not because he believes it. Reservation and marvel sit in the same paragraph, written by the same hand.

## What This Shifts

We readily put doubt toward sacred narratives on the side of the Moderns, and credulity on the side of the Ancients, as if no one, before the Enlightenment or the philology of the 19th century, had known how to read a myth without believing in it. Herodotus's text says the opposite, and says it from inside the very account it transmits: mistrust did not wait twenty-two centuries to be written down, it is already there in the work presented as the beginning of history as a discipline, the Greek word he chooses to name it, *historiē*, designating an inquiry, not a profession of faith.

Doubt, moreover, does not prevent transmission: it doubles it. Herodotus could have kept silent about what he does not believe; he chooses to write it while flagging it as doubtful, and it is this version, account and reservation together, that has traveled twenty-five centuries to reach us. What we read today in Herodotus about the phoenix (the extremely rare bird that comes only once every five hundred years) reaches us from a text that, at the very moment it fixes the legend in writing, refuses to subscribe to it.

citation.texte: What is told of this bird does not seem credible to me.

carte.punch: Herodotus reports the Egyptian phoenix, and warns that he himself does not believe it.
carte.idee: Around 450 BCE, Herodotus reports the Heliopolitan account of the phoenix, which comes to Egypt only once every five hundred years, and judges this account hardly credible. Doubt toward sacred narratives is not a modern invention: it is in the text that transmits the myth.

quiz.question: Why does Herodotus report the account of the phoenix while saying he does not believe it?
choix: Because passing on what he is told is part of his inquiry, distinct from personal belief
Because religious censorship prevented him from deleting the passage
Because he had himself seen the bird and wanted to describe his mistake
Because the account had been imposed on him by the priests of Heliopolis under oath
quiz.explication: Herodotus distinguishes what he is told from what he believes: reporting is part of his inquiry (historiē), believing is not. He never saw the bird, no censorship is at play, and no oath frames his work of collecting.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the account reported by Herodotus, on what occasion does the phoenix come to Egypt?
choix: Every year, at the summer solstice
Once every five hundred years, at the death of its father
Only once, at the very beginning of the world
Each time a new pharaoh ascends the throne
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The account sets a five-hundred-year cycle, at the death of the bird's father: neither an annual rhythm, nor a single event at the origin of the world, nor a link with a pharaoh's accession.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Herodotus say about the provenance of what he reports, in a passage of his Histories on the Argives (VII, 152)?
choix: That he is bound to report what he is told, without being bound to believe it
That he refuses to pass on any account he judges implausible
That he reports only what he has seen with his own eyes
That he always lets his readers judge without ever giving his own opinion
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Herodotus extends to his whole inquiry the principle he applies to the phoenix: reporting what he is told does not oblige him to believe it. He therefore does not refuse implausible accounts, does not report only what he saw, and does give his own opinion, as with the phoenix.
